policy_name: Fixed Period of Admission for F Nonimmigrants
current_policy: F–1 nonimmigrant students are admitted for Duration of Status (D/S), meaning the length necessary to complete the course of study without a fixed end date, with opportunities for program extensions granted by DSOs.
proposed_change: DHS proposes to change admission of F–1 nonimmigrants from D/S to a fixed period of admission, limited to the length of the student's educational program, not to exceed 4 years. Extensions of stay (EOS) applications must be adjudicated by immigration officers who would review compliance with visa status requirements and admissibility.
plain_english: Instead of letting F–1 students stay in the U.S. for as long as their studies take, DHS wants to limit their stay to a fixed time (up to 4 years), after which they must apply for extensions that DHS officers will review more closely.
allowed: Program extensions recommended by DSOs
EOS applications adjudicated by DHS officers
Continuation in full course of study
Medical or academic reasons for extension with proper adjudication
restricted_or_prohibited: Unlimited enrollment through repeated program extensions without DHS review
DSOs solely granting program extensions without DHS adjudication
time_limits_or_durations: Fixed admission period up to 4 years
Extensions beyond initial fixed period require DHS adjudication
evidence_quote: DHS believes it can mitigate fraud risks in part through, as this rule proposes, setting the authorized admission and extension periods for F nonimmigrants as the length of the F nonimmigrant’s specific program, not to exceed a 4-year period. It would establish a mechanism for immigration officers to assess these nonimmigrants at defined periods (such as when applying for an EOS in the United States beyond a 4-year admission period) and determine whether they are complying with the conditions of their classification.

policy_name: Fixed Period of Admission for J Nonimmigrants
current_policy: J–1 exchange visitors are admitted for Duration of Status (D/S), meaning the duration of their exchange visitor program without a fixed end date, with program extensions authorized by Responsible Officers (ROs) under Department of State regulations, and USCIS adjudicates EOS applications based on those extensions.
proposed_change: DHS proposes to change the admission of J–1 exchange visitors from D/S to a fixed period of admission limited to the length of the exchange visitor’s specific program, not to exceed 4 years, requiring immigration officers to adjudicate EOS applications and verify compliance.
plain_english: J–1 exchange visitors will be admitted for a limited fixed time (up to 4 years) instead of as long as their program lasts, so DHS officers can periodically check if they are complying with visa conditions.
allowed: Program extensions recommended by ROs
EOS applications adjudicated by DHS officers
Continuation of exchange program within fixed period
restricted_or_prohibited: Unlimited D/S admission without defined expiration
Extensions beyond maximum without proper adjudication
exceptions: Extensions beyond maximum durations must be approved by DOS
time_limits_or_durations: Fixed admission period up to 4 years
Maximum program durations per 22 CFR: 5 years for professors and research scholars, 7 years for alien physicians
evidence_quote: DHS believes that the national security risks posed by D/S admissions for individuals admitted under the J classification are similar to those posed by the F classification. ... setting the length of the J nonimmigrant’s specific program to not exceed a 4-year period would establish a mechanism for immigration officers to assess these nonimmigrants at defined periods (such as when applying for an EOS in the United States beyond a 4-year admission period) and determine whether they are complying with the conditions of their classification.

policy_name: Fixed Period of Admission for I Nonimmigrants
affected_groups: I nonimmigrant representatives of foreign information media
current_policy: I nonimmigrant foreign media representatives are admitted for Duration of Status (D/S) tied to the duration of their employment, except those with passports from the People’s Republic of China, who have different rules. Changes to D/S admissions were proposed in 2020 but withdrawn in 2021.
proposed_change: DHS proposes to replace admission for D/S with admission for a fixed period of admission for I nonimmigrants, similar to F and J nonimmigrants, requiring periodic DHS adjudication to extend stay based on program continuation and compliance.
plain_english: Foreign media representatives will be admitted for a specific fixed time period instead of simply for as long as they work, so DHS can regularly check if they meet admission conditions.
allowed: Employment-related stay within fixed admission period
Extensions upon DHS review and approval
restricted_or_prohibited: D/S admission without fixed end date
exceptions: Current exception for PRC passport holders noted but no change detailed
time_limits_or_durations: Fixed admission period with specific duration to be set
evidence_quote: Through its administration of the regulations authorizing I nonimmigrants admission for duration of employment, DHS currently admits all I nonimmigrants for D/S with the exception of those presenting a passport issued by the People’s Republic of China (other than a Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR) passport or a Macau SAR passport). Changes to D/S were proposed for I foreign media representatives in 2020, but the proposal was withdrawn in 2021.

policy_name: Separation of Program Extension and Extension of Stay (EOS) Adjudications
current_policy: DSOs (for F–1) and ROs (for J–1) have authority to grant program extensions (academic or exchange visitor program) and report to DHS. DHS currently does not adjudicate the extension of stay as a separate immigration benefit except when USCIS approves EOS applications for J–1.
proposed_change: DHS proposes to separate the determination of program extension (recommended by DSOs/ROs) from adjudicating an extension of stay application by immigration officers. The immigration officers will have discretion to verify eligibility and compliance before approving EOS.
plain_english: Schools and sponsors will still recommend extensions to programs, but DHS immigration officers will make the final decision to allow foreign students or visitors to stay longer, giving DHS direct oversight and the ability to verify compliance.
allowed: DSO/RO recommendation of program extension
Immigration officer adjudication of EOS applications
restricted_or_prohibited: DSO/RO sole authority to extend stay without DHS review
evidence_quote: DHS believes that the determinations of program extension and EOS should be separated, with the DSO’s and RO’s recommendation being one factor an immigration officer reviews while adjudicating an application for EOS. Changing to a fixed period of admission would give immigration officers a mechanism to make this evaluation at reasonably frequent intervals.

policy_name: Increased Biometrics and Admissibility Checks at EOS Application for F and J Nonimmigrants
current_policy: F–1 students admitted under D/S do not generally apply for or have their EOS applications adjudicated by DHS and may lack biometrics or admissibility adjudications during program extensions by DSOs. J–1 extensions handled by DOS sponsors and USCIS adjudicates EOS applications based on approved program extensions.
proposed_change: DHS proposes to collect biometrics and conduct admissibility checks at EOS application for F and J nonimmigrants under fixed admission periods. Failure to meet admissibility grounds will result in denial of EOS.
plain_english: When F–1 and J–1 students or visitors want to extend their stay beyond the fixed admission period, they will have to provide biometrics and prove they are admissible, helping DHS identify and prevent fraud or security risks.
allowed: EOS applications subject to DHS biometrics and admissibility checks
restricted_or_prohibited: Program extensions without DHS biometric or admissibility review
time_limits_or_durations: 24 to 48 months, generally up to 4 years initial period before requiring EOS adjudication
evidence_quote: Significantly, under the proposed changes to the period of admission of F nonimmigrants and the applicable EOS process, DHS would collect biometrics and other information (such as evidence of financial resources to cover expenses and evidence of any criminal activity) from F nonimmigrant students more frequently, thereby enhancing the Government’s oversight and monitoring of these aliens.

policy_name: Fixed Admission Period for F and J Nonimmigrants
current_policy: F and J nonimmigrants are admitted for Duration of Status (D/S) without a fixed period.
proposed_change: Replace Duration of Status admissions with a fixed admission period of up to 4 years or the specified program end date on Form I–20 or DS–2019, whichever is shorter, plus 30 days arrival and 30 days departure periods. Aliens must apply for an extension of stay (EOS) to remain beyond this period. Specific rules govern admission when aliens depart and later seek readmission.
plain_english: Students and exchange visitors will no longer get indefinite stay linked to their program status; instead, they'll be allowed to stay for a set time (up to 4 years) plus some extra days before and after. To stay longer, they have to apply for an extension.
allowed: Admission up to 4 years or program end date, whichever is shorter
30-day period before program start date for arrival
30-day period after program end date for preparation/departure
Applying for an EOS to extend stay
Admission after absence up to 30 days in contiguous territory or adjacent islands (visa revalidation)
restricted_or_prohibited: Admission for Duration of Status (D/S) removed
Unlawful presence accrual begins after fixed admission period expires
Failure to apply for EOS when staying beyond period
Relying exclusively on Responsible Officials for program extensions
exceptions: F and J nonimmigrants admitted for D/S on the final rule’s effective date may continue until program end date on Form I–20 or DS–2019 up to 4 years plus respective departure periods (transition provision)
Specific provisions for aliens applying for admission while EOS applications are pending
Aliens in F status filing timely applications for post-completion OPT or STEM OPT within 6 months after rule effective date are not required to file EOS for employment authorization during transition
time_limits_or_durations: Maximum 4-year fixed admission period or program end date on Form I–20/DS–2019, whichever is shorter
30 days before program start date for arrival
30-day period after program end date for departure
60 days departure period for F nonimmigrants after admission period
30 days departure period for J nonimmigrants after admission period
evidence_quote: DHS proposes changes to the admission provisions for these particular nonimmigrant classifications, including replacing admissions for "duration of status" with a fixed admission period... Under this proposal, aliens applying for admission in either F or J status would be eligible to be admitted for a maximum period of 4 years or the length of program as specified on Form I–20 or DS–2019, whichever is shorter, or the end date of the approved employment authorization for post-completion OPT and Science Technology Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) OPT, as applicable, plus additional 30 day periods for arrival and a 30-day period to prepare for departure... See proposed 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i) through (iii); and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5) and (j)(1)(ii).

policy_name: Fixed Admission Period for J Exchange Visitors (College and University Students)
affected_groups: J–1 college and university students (exchange visitors)
current_policy: J–1 exchange visitor students are admitted for Duration of Status (D/S); program extensions handled by Responsible Officers without DHS adjudication or admissibility checks.
proposed_change: Require J–1 college and university students to be admitted for a fixed period instead of D/S, matching the fixed admission period approach for F–1 students (up to 4 years). EOS applications would require DHS adjudication including admissibility checks and biometrics collection.
plain_english: College and university students on J–1 visas will get a set stay period instead of indefinite status. They must apply to DHS to extend their stay, allowing DHS to do background checks and confirm the student’s legitimacy.
allowed: Admission for fixed period up to 4 years or program length
Collection of biometrics during EOS
DHS vetting and admissibility determinations upon EOS
restricted_or_prohibited: Admission for Duration of Status (D/S) removed for J–1 students
Responsibility for program extensions shifted from Responsible Officers to DHS
Extension of program without DHS review no longer allowed
time_limits_or_durations: Up to 4 years or program end date, whichever is shorter
30-day periods before start and after program end for arrival and departure respectively
evidence_quote: By requiring the same fixed period of admission for F–1s and J–1s, J–1 college and university students in exchange visitor programs would be unable to circumvent the intent of this proposed rule... Switching from D/S to a fixed period of admission would permit immigration officers the opportunity to determine whether an alien is eligible for an additional period of time. ... Under the proposed changes to the period of admission of J exchange visitors and the applicable EOS process, DHS would more frequently collect biometrics and other information from J exchange visitors, enhancing the Government’s oversight and monitoring of these aliens.

policy_name: Fixed Admission Period and Extension of Stay for I Nonimmigrants
affected_groups: I nonimmigrants (representatives of foreign information media)
current_policy: I nonimmigrants and their dependents admitted for Duration of Status (D/S).
proposed_change: Replace D/S with fixed admission period for I nonimmigrants. Individuals wishing to remain beyond the authorized stay must apply for an Extension of Stay (EOS) with USCIS and submit specified evidence supporting the EOS request.
plain_english: Foreign media representatives will now be admitted for a set time, not an indefinite period matching their ‘status duration.’ To stay longer, they must apply for an extension with DHS and provide evidence of their eligible activities.
allowed: Admission for a fixed period
Applying for EOS with DHS
Providing evidence supporting the purpose of stay during EOS
restricted_or_prohibited: Admission for Duration of Status (D/S) removed
Staying beyond fixed admitted period without approved EOS prohibited
exceptions: The proposed changes to additional evidentiary requirements would apply to a nonimmigrant in the United States who requests to change to I nonimmigrant status.
evidence_quote: The Department believes admitting aliens temporarily in the United States for a fixed period would strengthen vetting and information collection and help immigration officers ensure that the I nonimmigrants are, and will be, engaged in activities that are permissible under INA 101(a)(15)(I). In addition, this rulemaking proposes to require individuals who wish to remain in I nonimmigrant status beyond the end date for their authorized stay to apply for an EOS with USCIS, at which point immigration officers can review their activities in the United States. It also clarifies what DHS would require these individuals to present as evidence supporting their EOS request.

policy_name: Extension of Stay Procedure and Requirements for F, J, and I Nonimmigrants
current_policy: F and J nonimmigrants not required to file for EOS to extend stay; program extensions handled by DSOs or Responsible Officers without DHS adjudication and without biometric requirements. I nonimmigrants admitted with D/S and also not required to file EOS.
proposed_change: Require F, J, and I nonimmigrants to file an EOS with USCIS if they wish to remain beyond their fixed admission date. The regulatory text will remove references exempting F and J from EOS filing requirements. USCIS will require biometric collection and may require interviews as part of EOS adjudication. Also, references to specific forms (I–129, I–539) replaced with general applicable language to allow form changes without rulemaking.
plain_english: Students, exchange visitors, and foreign media representatives must now file for an extension with DHS if they want to stay beyond a set period, and they will have to provide biometrics and possibly go to interviews.
allowed: Application for EOS using forms designated by USCIS
Biometric collection and possible interviews as part of EOS
USCIS adjudication of EOS including admissibility review
restricted_or_prohibited: F and J nonimmigrants exempted from EOS filing no longer exempt
Failure to file EOS when required will result in status violation
No appeal allowed of EOS denial
exceptions: Certain nonimmigrants admitted for D/S like A–1 and A–2 representatives of foreign governments and their families remain ineligible to file EOS and thus exempt
evidence_quote: Therefore, DHS proposes to use this language in 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2) and to strike the current phrase exempting F and J nonimmigrants from the requirement to file an EOS, as they would be required to file an EOS if they wish to remain in the United States beyond their specified date of admission. ... As part of the EOS application, USCIS requires biometric collection and will require such collection from F, J, and I nonimmigrants under the proposed rule. ... USCIS may require such an interview as part of the screening and adjudication process that helps confirm an individual’s identity, elicit information to assess the eligibility for an immigration benefit, and screen for any national security or fraud concerns.

policy_name: EOS Application Abandonment and Admission Upon Departure and Readmission
affected_groups: F, J, and I nonimmigrants who file EOS
current_policy: EOS applications are generally not considered abandoned upon departure; an alien may remain in status under D/S until the EOS is adjudicated.
proposed_change: If an alien in F, J, or I status timely files an EOS and departs before USCIS approves it, and then applies for admission to continue stay for the balance of the previously authorized admission period, the EOS application generally is NOT considered abandoned. However, if the alien departs and applies for admission while EOS is pending and is admitted for a new fixed admission period based on a new Form I–20 or DS–2019, the pending EOS will be considered abandoned, and the CBP-issued admission period controls.
plain_english: Flying out after filing to stay longer usually doesn’t cancel the extension request, unless the person comes back and is admitted for a new stay period based on a new program document; then the old extension request is canceled.
allowed: Leaving U.S. after timely EOS filing without abandoning EOS in some cases
Reapplying for admission for balance of previously authorized stay
restricted_or_prohibited: EOS considered abandoned if alien is admitted for a new fixed period during pending EOS
Not responding timely to Requests for Evidence (RFE) while abroad can lead to denial for abandonment
evidence_quote: Where an alien in F, J, or I status timely files an application for EOS, leaves the United States before USCIS approves that EOS application, and applies for admission to continue his or her activities for the balance of the previously authorized admission period, USCIS would generally not consider the EOS application abandoned. ... Where the alien leaves the United States and applies for admission while his or her EOS application is pending and is admitted based on a new Form I–20 or DS–2019 after his or her previously authorized admission has expired, the pending EOS is deemed abandoned. In this case, the admit until date provided by CBP on the alien’s I–94 would govern.

policy_name: Transition Period for F and J Nonimmigrants Currently Admitted for D/S
affected_groups: F and J nonimmigrants admitted for Duration of Status (D/S) on the final rule’s effective date
current_policy: Such nonimmigrants admitted for D/S remain in status until program completion without fixed admission period and without EOS filing.
proposed_change: Allow these F and J nonimmigrants to remain in status without filing EOS until the program end date on their Form I–20 or DS–2019 in effect on the rule’s effective date, not to exceed 4 years from the effective date, plus 60 days (F) or 30 days (J) to depart. After departure, admission would be with fixed admission periods and EOS requirements. Timely filed applications for post-completion OPT or STEM OPT within 6 months after the effective date are not required to file EOS during transition.
plain_english: People already here under the old system can stay until their current program’s end date (up to 4 years maximum) plus some extra days. After they leave and try to come back, they must follow the new fixed stay rules.
allowed: Remaining in status without filing EOS until program end date or 4 years from effective date plus departure periods
Filing post-completion OPT or STEM OPT employment authorization applications without EOS in certain transition circumstances
restricted_or_prohibited: Failure to file timely EOS after transition period ends
Departing and reentering triggers fixed admission periods and EOS rules
exceptions: F–1 nonimmigrants present 60 days after final rule publication and timely filing applications for post-completion OPT or STEM OPT within 6 months after effective date need not file EOS immediately
time_limits_or_durations: Up to 4 years from final rule effective date
60-day departure period for F nonimmigrants
30-day departure period for J nonimmigrants
evidence_quote: DHS proposes to generally allow all F and J nonimmigrants present in the United States on the final rule’s effective date who are validly maintaining that status and who were admitted for D/S to remain in the United States in F or J status, without filing an EOS request, up to the program end date reflected on their Form I–20 or DS–2019 that is valid on the Final Rule’s effective date, for a period not to exceed 4 years from the effective date of the Final Rule, plus an additional 60 days for these F nonimmigrants and 30 days for J nonimmigrants to depart the country. ... For those aliens in F–1 status... timely filed on or before 6 months after the effective date of the final rule for an application for post-completion OPT or a STEM OPT extension, there would not be a requirement to file an EOS application, and, instead, they would be required to file the application for employment authorization for post-completion OPT or a STEM OPT extension.

policy_name: Change of Language and Discretion in Visa Revalidation for Contiguous Travel
affected_groups: F, J, and M nonimmigrants traveling in contiguous territory or adjacent islands for up to 30 days
current_policy: Visa revalidation provisions use the word ‘shall’ regarding DHS admitting aliens and extending visa validity automatically for contiguous territory travel, potentially implying mandatory admission.
proposed_change: Change regulatory language from ‘shall’ to ‘may’ in visa revalidation provisions to clarify that CBP officers have discretionary authority to decide admissibility and period of admission, including automatic visa validity extension upon re-entry from contiguous territory or adjacent islands for excursions not exceeding 30 days.
plain_english: CBP officers will have discretion to decide whether to admit nonimmigrants who return automatically from nearby travel even if the visa is expired, rather than being required to admit them.
allowed: Automatic extension of visa validity at port of entry for absence of up to 30 days in contiguous territory or adjacent islands
CBP discretion in admitting aliens and determining period of admission
restricted_or_prohibited: Remove any implication that CBP must admit aliens automatically
time_limits_or_durations: Absence not exceeding 30 days in contiguous territory or adjacent islands
evidence_quote: DHS proposes to change the admission language in the provision relating to extension of visa validity in limited situations from "shall" to "may" to clarify that CBP always maintains the discretion to determine whether an alien is admissible and the appropriate period of admission. ... These provisions apply when, for example, a nonimmigrant finds himself or herself applying for re-entry after going to Mexico on spring break without realizing that his or her visa had expired. Instead of having to get a new visa, CBP may admit the nonimmigrant, whose visa validity is automatically extended by operation of DOS regulations. See 22 CFR 41.112(d).

policy_name: Removal of References to Obsolete or Inapplicable Immigration Classifications and Terms
current_policy: Regulations reference the obsolete INA 101(a)(15)(Q)(ii) classification and include references to Duration of Status in admission provisions.
proposed_change: Strike the reference to INA 101(a)(15)(Q)(ii), which no longer exists, and remove references to Duration of Status in 8 CFR 214.1(b)(1), 214.2(f)(5)(vii), 214.2(f)(18)(iii), and 274a.12(b)(6)(v).
plain_english: The rule removes outdated immigration category references and the use of 'Duration of Status' which will no longer apply under the proposed changes.
restricted_or_prohibited: Use of obsolete INA 101(a)(15)(Q)(ii) classification
References to 'Duration of Status' in certain regulations
evidence_quote: DHS proposes to strike the reference to INA 101(a)(15)(Q)(ii) and reserve it, as that program no longer exists and is no longer in the INA. ... DHS proposes to strike the reference to "duration of status" in 8 CFR 214.1(b)(1), 214.2(f)(5)(vii), 214.2(f)(18)(iii), and 274a.12(b)(6)(v).

policy_name: Transition from Duration of Status (D/S) to Fixed Admission Period for F and J Nonimmigrants
current_policy: F and J nonimmigrants admitted for D/S can remain lawfully in the U.S. for the duration of their program plus any authorized practical training and a subsequent grace period.
proposed_change: DHS proposes to eliminate D/S admissions, replacing them with a fixed admission period that uses the program end date on the Form I–20 or DS–2019, with a maximum period not to exceed 4 years, plus an additional 60 days for F nonimmigrants and 30 days for J nonimmigrants to remain in the U.S. without filing an extension of stay (EOS). Nonimmigrants wishing to extend stay beyond this fixed period or the program end date must file an EOS or depart and reapply at a port of entry.
plain_english: Instead of letting students stay in the U.S. for 'duration of status,' they will get a fixed admission end date based on their program end date with some extra days. If they want to stay longer, they must apply for an extension or leave and come back legally.
allowed: Remaining in the U.S. until program end date + 60 days (F) or +30 days (J) without EOS application
Applying for EOS to extend stay beyond fixed admission period
restricted_or_prohibited: Remaining indefinitely in the U.S. under D/S without fixed end date
Retaining D/S admission after expiration of fixed admission period without approved EOS
exceptions: Certain J-1 research scholars and alien physicians with programs longer than 4 years need to apply for EOS before the 4-year limit expires
Transition procedures do not apply to aliens outside the U.S. or in violation of status at effective date
time_limits_or_durations: Fixed admission not to exceed 4 years
Plus 60 days for F nonimmigrants
Plus 30 days for J nonimmigrants
evidence_quote: DHS’s proposal is to transition all F and J nonimmigrants to a fixed admission date by using the program end date noted on their Form I–20 or DS–2019 (with the exception of F students engaging in post-completion or a STEM OPT extension who would use their EAD’s expiration date), not to exceed 4 years, plus an additional 60 days for F nonimmigrants and 30 days for J nonimmigrants as provided in their previous admission.

policy_name: Automatic Extension and Extension of Stay (EOS) Procedures for I Nonimmigrants
current_policy: I nonimmigrants admitted under D/S have indefinite duration; must file EOS via Form I-539 if sought.
proposed_change: DHS proposes an automatic extension of I nonimmigrants' admission up to 240 days past the expiration date to complete activities, based on a filing of extension of stay request. If an extension is denied, the individual must cease employment and depart immediately with no grace period.
plain_english: I nonimmigrants will get automatic extra time (up to 240 days) to finish their assignment if they file for an extension, but must leave immediately if the extension is denied.
allowed: Automatic 240-day extension of stay following expiration of status with timely filed extension request
Working during extension period pending approval
restricted_or_prohibited: Continuing employment or stay after denial of extension request
Departure grace period after denial
time_limits_or_durations: Up to 240 days automatic extension
evidence_quote: DHS proposes an automatic extension of the length of time it takes the alien to complete his or her activity, for a period of up to 240 days. See proposed 8 CFR 214.1(m)(3).

policy_name: Admission Period for F Nonimmigrants Limited to 4 Years
current_policy: F nonimmigrants admitted for Duration of Status (D/S), allowing stay for the length of their program plus authorized practical training and grace periods without a fixed maximum time limit.
proposed_change: DHS proposes to eliminate D/S and admit F nonimmigrants for the length of their program up to a maximum of 4 years. Students must apply for EOS if they wish to remain beyond that.
plain_english: F-1 students will have their stay limited to a maximum of 4 years per admission; to stay longer, they need to apply for an extension.
allowed: Enrollment in programs up to 4 years
Applying for extension of stay beyond 4 years
restricted_or_prohibited: Admission for D/S (no fixed end date)
Stay beyond 4 years without EOS application
time_limits_or_durations: Up to 4 years admission period
evidence_quote: DHS is proposing to strike the existing regulation that allows F nonimmigrants to be admitted for D/S. DHS would replace it with a provision allowing F nonimmigrants to be granted status for the length of their program, not to exceed 4 years. See proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i) and (f)(7)(vi).

policy_name: Aggregate Language Study Limit of 24 Months for F-1 Students in Language Training Programs
affected_groups: F-1 students enrolled in language training programs
current_policy: No aggregate limit on length of language study for F-1 students.
proposed_change: DHS proposes limiting F-1 students attending language training programs to a maximum aggregate of 24 months including breaks and vacations to prevent abusive long-term enrollment in language schools.
plain_english: F-1 students can study English or other language training for up to 24 months total; after that, they cannot remain in F-1 status for language training.
allowed: Aggregate language study up to 24 months
restricted_or_prohibited: Language training in F-1 status beyond 24 months aggregate
time_limits_or_durations: 24 months aggregate limit for language study
evidence_quote: F–1 students in a language training program would be restricted to an aggregate of 24 months of language study, which would include breaks and an annual vacation. See proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(A).

policy_name: Retention of Authorized Stay for F-1 Students with Pending EAD Applications Beyond EAD Expiration
affected_groups: F-1 students with post-completion or STEM OPT pending EAD applications
current_policy: F-1 students must maintain valid EAD to remain authorized for employment and lawful status.
proposed_change: F-1 students with pending EAD applications who cease employment due to EAD expiration before the program end date may remain in authorized stay until the fixed admission end date noted on their Form I-94, unless they violate status.
plain_english: F-1 students waiting on employment authorization can stay lawfully in the U.S. beyond their EAD expiration until their program end date or fixed admission end date.
allowed: Remaining authorized to stay from EAD expiration to fixed admission end date if EAD renewal is pending
restricted_or_prohibited: Employment without valid EAD
Violating terms of authorized stay
time_limits_or_durations: Period from EAD expiration to fixed admission end date
evidence_quote: F–1 students with pending employment authorization applications who are admitted based on the DSO’s recommended employment end date for post-completion OPT or STEM OPT specified on their Form I–20 ... be considered to be in the United States in a period of authorized stay from the date of the expiration noted on their EAD until the fixed date of admission as noted on their I–94 (unless the student violates the terms of the authorized stay).

policy_name: F-1 Dependents' Stay Limited to Principal's Authorized Stay
current_policy: F-2 dependents' authorized period of stay is tied to that of the principal F-1 alien but not explicitly included in regulatory text.
proposed_change: DHS proposes expressly adding a requirement that F-2 dependents' authorized stay not exceed that of the principal F-1 alien in regulation.
plain_english: F-2 dependents cannot stay longer than the F-1 student they depend on.
allowed: Authorized stay concurrent with principal F-1 alien
restricted_or_prohibited: Period of stay for F-2 dependents exceeding principal's stay
time_limits_or_durations: Not to exceed principal F-1 alien's stay
evidence_quote: The authorized period of stay for F–2 dependents will continue to not be able to exceed the authorized period of stay of the principal F–1 alien. DHS proposes adding this requirement to 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(E).

policy_name: Restrictions on Change of Educational Objectives and Transfers for F-1 Students
current_policy: All changes in education level or multiple degrees within the same level are considered maintaining status with no limits.
proposed_change: DHS proposes to restrict school transfers and changes in educational objectives within the first academic year unless authorized by SEVP, prohibit graduate-level F-1 students from changing educational objectives or transferring within the U.S., disallow maintaining F-1 status after completion of a program at one educational level through enrollment in same or lower-level programs, allow progress only to higher educational levels, and require EOS application for changes in education level that require extension.
plain_english: F-1 students will have limits on transferring schools or changing majors especially within the first year, cannot downgrade education levels, and must progress upward academically to keep status.
allowed: Transfers or changes after first academic year with SEVP authorization
Progressing to a higher educational level program
restricted_or_prohibited: Transfers or changes within first academic year without authorization
Transferring or changing educational objectives for graduate students within U.S.
Maintaining status by enrolling in same or lower educational level after program completion
exceptions: Exceptions authorized by SEVP for extenuating circumstances (e.g., school closure, prolonged inability to hold classes)
time_limits_or_durations: First academic year restriction period
evidence_quote: DHS proposes to restrict school transfers and changes of educational objectives within a student’s first academic year of a program of study, unless an exception is authorized by SEVP, and to prohibit F–1 students in a graduate level program of study from changing educational objectives or transferring from within the United States... An alien who has completed a program as an F–1 nonimmigrant at one educational level would be unable to maintain F–1 status...through a program at the same educational level or a lower educational level.

policy_name: Reduction of Departure Preparation Period for F-1 Students from 60 Days to 30 Days
current_policy: F-1 students are granted 60 days after completion of studies or practical training to prepare for departure, apply for extensions, or change status.
proposed_change: DHS proposes reducing the post-completion departure preparation period for F-1 students from 60 to 30 days to align more closely with J and M nonimmigrant categories and establish uniformity. This time can be used to prepare for departure or file for EOS or change of status.
plain_english: F-1 students will now have 30 days instead of 60 days after finishing studies to get ready to leave the U.S. or apply for extensions or status changes.
allowed: Using 30-day period to prepare for departure
Seeking timely extensions of stay or change of status during period
restricted_or_prohibited: Departure preparation beyond 30 days without extension approval
exceptions: Current 15-day departure period retained for students authorized to withdraw from classes
time_limits_or_durations: 30 days after Form I-94 or EAD expiration
evidence_quote: DHS believes that the time allotted for F students to prepare for departure should be revised from 60 to 30 days. See 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(iv) and proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v).

policy_name: Reduction of post-completion grace period for F-1 students
current_policy: F-1 students have 60 days to maintain legal status or depart the United States after completing their program or post-completion OPT
proposed_change: Reduce the 60-day period to 30 days after completion of studies or authorized practical training
plain_english: After finishing their studies or training, F-1 students would have 30 days to either apply for extensions or leave instead of the current 60 days
allowed: Take steps necessary to maintain legal status or depart the United States within 30 days
restricted_or_prohibited: Use of 60-day grace period
time_limits_or_durations: 30 days after completion of studies or post-completion OPT
evidence_quote: Per existing regulations, after completing their program or post-completion OPT, F–1 students have 60 days (which DHS is proposing to change to 30 days) to take the steps necessary to maintain legal status or depart the United States.

policy_name: Automatic extension of F-1 status and employment authorization during EOS application pendency
affected_groups: F-1 nonimmigrant students with timely filed EOS applications
current_policy: F-1 students admitted for duration of status and their employment authorizations generally expire with the period of admission. On-campus employment can continue under DSO authorization; however, employment authorizations require separate approval.
proposed_change: Authorize automatic extension of F-1 status and related employment authorization (including on-campus employment and off-campus employment based on severe economic hardship) for up to 240 days while EOS applications are pending
plain_english: If an F-1 student files for an extension of stay before their status expires, their status and some types of employment authorization would automatically extend up to 240 days during processing
allowed: On-campus employment up to 240 days during EOS pendency
Off-campus employment for severe economic hardship up to 240 days during EOS pendency
SSR employment authorization extended automatically up to the Federal Register notice end date or 240 days, whichever is earlier
restricted_or_prohibited: Employment authorization ceases if EOS pending beyond 240 days
exceptions: SSR employment limited not to exceed the F-1 student’s academic program end date
time_limits_or_durations: 240 days automatic extension period
evidence_quote: DHS proposes to allow aliens in F–1 status to continue to be authorized for on-campus employment while their EOS applications with USCIS are pending, not to exceed a period of 240 days... DHS is proposing an automatic extension of off-campus employment authorization for up to 240-days during the pendency of the EOS application... DHS proposes to automatically extend SSR authorization if an F–1 alien has a timely-filed EOS pending for up to the end date stated in the Federal Register notice..., or 240 days, whichever is earlier.

policy_name: Requirement for F-1 students to file EOS applications with USCIS for program extensions instead of DSO approval alone
affected_groups: F-1 nonimmigrant students seeking program extensions
current_policy: DSOs may grant program extensions based on a standard of 'normal progress' with no USCIS adjudication
proposed_change: Eliminate 'normal progress' standard and require F-1 students to obtain a DSO recommendation AND submit an EOS application to USCIS with proof of compelling academic reasons, documented medical illness, or exceptional circumstances beyond the student's control for an extension beyond approved admission period
plain_english: Instead of just getting approval from their school official, F-1 students must now file an extension request with USCIS supported by documented reasons (such as medical issues or emergencies) for extra time to complete their studies
allowed: Extension requests based on compelling academic reasons
Extension requests based on documented medical conditions
Extension requests based on exceptional circumstances beyond control (e.g., natural disasters, school closures)
restricted_or_prohibited: Program extensions solely based on undefined 'normal progress'
Program extensions for students repeatedly failing classes
Extensions for students without proper authorization for reduced course loads
exceptions: Exceptions exist for students authorized to drop below full course of study and those reinstated after loss of status
time_limits_or_durations: Extensions may not exceed 4 years except for border commuters, language training students, or public high school attendees
evidence_quote: Therefore, DHS proposes not to use a 'normal progress' standard with respect to seeking a program extension of an authorized period of stay... Instead, an alien... would be required to file an EOS application to request additional time... only if the additional time needed is due to a compelling academic reason, documented medical illness or medical condition, or circumstance that was beyond the student’s control.

policy_name: Direct USCIS adjudication for F-1 status extensions with evidence requirements
affected_groups: F-1 nonimmigrant students applying for extensions of stay
current_policy: DSOs grant program extensions; USCIS does not directly adjudicate extension requests except for reinstatements
proposed_change: USCIS would directly adjudicate EOS applications for program extensions requiring supporting evidence such as medical documentation, transcripts, and proof of financial support; USCIS may request additional information and grants extensions only when eligibility criteria are met
plain_english: USCIS officers will now review and decide on F-1 status extensions with submitted evidence, ensuring students meet requirements and are maintaining lawful status
allowed: Requests supported by medical documentation from licensed professionals
Requests supported by evidence of sufficient financial resources for study
restricted_or_prohibited: Extensions denied if student fails to maintain status, fails classes repeatedly, or lacks required evidence
exceptions: Students properly authorized to reduce course load and those reinstated may still be eligible
time_limits_or_durations: Extensions up to 4 years generally
evidence_quote: Immigration officers thereby would be able to conduct appropriate background and security checks... and directly review the proffered evidence... DHS proposes to codify standards already included in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(6)(iii)(B), which require a student to provide medical documentation from a licensed medical doctor... Applicants would need to submit evidence of sufficient funds to cover expenses.

policy_name: Requirement for timely filing of EOS applications by F-1 students and their dependents
affected_groups: F-1 nonimmigrant students and F-2 dependents
current_policy: DSO program extensions do not require USCIS filing; dependents may not have separate EOS filing requirements
proposed_change: F-1 students must timely file EOS applications with USCIS on or before expiration of the authorized period including the 30-day grace period; F-2 dependents seeking to accompany the student must also file EOS or reinstatement applications as applicable
plain_english: Students and their dependents must file extension requests with USCIS before their current status expires to maintain legal status
allowed: Inclusion of dependents in primary EOS application or separate EOS applications with corresponding fees
restricted_or_prohibited: Late filing requires reinstatement applications; failure to maintain status results in ineligibility for EOS
exceptions: Late filing may be excused at USCIS discretion for extraordinary circumstances
time_limits_or_durations: On or before expiration of current authorized period including 30-day departure preparation period
evidence_quote: F–1 applicants generally would need to timely file their EOS application—meaning that USCIS would need to receive the application on or before the date the authorized admission period expires... F–2 dependents seeking to accompany the F–1 principal student would need to file applications for an EOS or reinstatement, as applicable.

policy_name: Immediate departure required after EOS denial without grace period
affected_groups: F-1 students and F-2 dependents whose EOS applications are denied
current_policy: No explicit mention of grace period; F nonimmigrants currently have a 60-day grace period after program completion
proposed_change: If USCIS denies an EOS application and the admission period has expired, the student and dependents must immediately depart the United States without any additional preparation time
plain_english: If extension applications are denied after status expires, students and their dependents must leave the country immediately with no extra days allowed
restricted_or_prohibited: Any stay beyond denial and expiration is prohibited and may result in unlawful presence
time_limits_or_durations: No grace period; immediate departure upon EOS denial and admission expiration
evidence_quote: If USCIS denies the request... and the period of admission for the student and his or her dependents has expired, then the student and his or her dependents would need to immediately depart the United States. As with other nonimmigrant classifications, they would not be given any period of time to prepare for departure...

policy_name: F-1 Student School Transfer and Program Change Conditions
current_policy: Aliens need to begin classes at the transfer school within 5 months of transferring or program completion date on Form I–20; must resume classes within 5 months if authorized for post-completion OPT. Failure to pursue a full course of study renders alien ineligible to change programs or transfer schools.
proposed_change: Retain the 5-month start class requirement post-transfer or program completion; clarify failure to pursue full course of study includes repeated inability or unwillingness; render ineligible for change of program or transfer if not maintaining full course load; clarify change to higher education level per transfer procedures; require EOS application if new program duration exceeds authorized admission period.
plain_english: F-1 students transferring schools or changing programs must start new classes within 5 months and maintain a full course load. If they don't, they're not allowed to change schools or programs without reinstatement. If new programs exceed the allowed stay, they must apply for an extension.
allowed: Transfer to new program within 5 months
Changes to higher education level following transfer procedures
Authorized participation in post-completion OPT with resume classes in 5 months
restricted_or_prohibited: Changing programs or transferring schools without full course of study
Using academic probation or suspension as a reason for program extension or failure to maintain full course load
exceptions: Reinstatement may be filed if eligible after failure to pursue full course of study
time_limits_or_durations: 5 months to begin classes after transfer or program completion
5 months to resume classes after OPT or changing programs
Program duration must not exceed authorized admission period unless EOS applied
evidence_quote: First, as is the case currently, aliens would need to begin classes at the transfer school or program within 5 months of transferring out of the current school or within 5 months of the program completion date on his or her current Form I–20; and second, if the alien is authorized to engage in post-completion OPT, he or she must be able to resume classes within 5 months of changing programs or transferring out of the school that recommended OPT or the date the OPT authorization ends, whichever is earlier. [...] DHS is proposing to retain the current provisions rendering aliens who do not pursue a full course of study ineligible to change programs or transfer schools, and is clarifying that failure to pursue a full course of study includes, but is not limited to, a student whose pattern of behavior demonstrates a repeated inability or unwillingness to complete his or her course of study. [...] Next, if the new program to which the student changes or transfers will not be completed within the authorized admission period established in paragraphs (f)(5)(i) of 8 CFR 214.2, then [...] the F–1 student would need to apply for EOS in the manner and on the form designated by USCIS, [...], with a valid, properly endorsed Form I–20 indicating the new program end date, and would need to provide biometrics as authorized by 8 CFR 103.16, if required.

policy_name: Elimination of Duration of Status (D/S) for Border Commuter Students
current_policy: Duration of status (D/S) does not apply to border commuter students.
proposed_change: Strike the provision referencing D/S is inapplicable to border commuter students due to elimination of D/S for all F nonimmigrants.
plain_english: Border commuter students will no longer be under the D/S rule because D/S is removed for all F visa holders.
restricted_or_prohibited: D/S is eliminated for all F nonimmigrants including border commuter students
evidence_quote: DHS proposes to strike the sentence referencing how ‘‘duration of status’’ is inapplicable to border commuter students because DHS is proposing to eliminate D/S for all F nonimmigrants.

policy_name: Maximum 4-Year Admission Period for J-1 Exchange Visitors
current_policy: Varied permissible initial time periods up to 5 years depending on category; program extensions possible with DOS approval.
proposed_change: Implement a uniform maximum initial period of admission not to exceed 4 years for all J-1 categories, aligning with F nonimmigrant maximum period.
plain_english: All J-1 visitors will have a maximum 4-year admission period regardless of category, similar to F visa holders.
allowed: Initial admission up to 4 years for all J-1 categories
restricted_or_prohibited: Admission periods exceeding 4 years
time_limits_or_durations: Maximum of 4 years admission period
evidence_quote: Under proposed 8 CFR 214.2(j)(1), J exchange visitors would be able to receive an initial period of admission not to exceed the program end date as stated on the Form DS–2019, up to a period of 4 years. [...] DHS is implementing the same 4-year maximum period of admission.

policy_name: 30-Day Preparation for Departure Period for J-1 Exchange Visitors
current_policy: Current regulations provide a 30-day period for travel or designated purposes before program start or after program end.
proposed_change: Retain 30-day period post-program end or 4-year maximum period, clarifying it is for departure or seeking to maintain lawful status (including filing EOS).
plain_english: J-1 visitors get 30 days after their program or 4-year limit to prepare to leave or apply to extend their stay.
allowed: 30 days after program end or 4-year max for departure or status maintenance
time_limits_or_durations: 30-day period from program end date or 4-year max period, whichever is earlier
evidence_quote: DHS proposes to retain the 30-day period that J nonimmigrants are provided before the report date or start of the approved program listed on the DS–2019 and the 30-day period for preparation for departure. [...] the Department proposes to revise the language [...] to instead read ‘‘a period of 30 days from the program end date or the 4-year maximum period of admission, whichever is earlier, for the purposes of departure or to otherwise seek to maintain lawful status.’’

policy_name: Limit on J-2 Dependent Extensions to Principal J-1 Period of Admission
affected_groups: J-2 spouses and children of J-1 principals
current_policy: Initial admission for J-2 dependents may not exceed principal J-1's authorized admission period.
proposed_change: Codify that extension of stay for J-2 dependents may not exceed the authorized admission period of the principal J-1.
plain_english: J-2 family members can only stay as long as the J-1 principal is authorized to stay.
allowed: Extensions for J-2 dependents up to principal J-1's admission period
restricted_or_prohibited: Extension beyond principal J-1's authorized admission period
time_limits_or_durations: No longer than principal J-1's authorized period
evidence_quote: DHS proposes to codify the policy that extensions for spouses or children who are granted J–2 status based on their derivative relationship as a spouse or child of the principal J–1 nonimmigrant may not exceed the period of authorized admission of the principal J–1. [...] the authorized period of initial admission for J–2 dependents would be subject to the same requirements as the J–1 exchange visitor and may not exceed the period of authorized admission of the principal J–1 exchange visitor.

policy_name: J-1 Exchange Visitor Extension of Stay (EOS) Application Process and Employment Authorization
affected_groups: J-1 exchange visitors and J-2 dependents
current_policy: J-1 extensions require RO and DOS approval; J-2 employment requires separate USCIS authorization; current provisions allow certain extensions and employment during pending EOS.
proposed_change: Require EOS application filed with USCIS with fee, form, and biometrics; J-1 program extensions through sponsor followed by EOS with USCIS; allow J–1s with timely filed EOS to continue authorized employment/training up to 240 days post-admission expiration; J–2 employment requires separate authorization with employment limited to supporting recreational/cultural activities, not J–1; deny J–2 EOS if J–1 EOS denied; allow J–1/J–2 travel without abandonment of EOS; require prompt departure upon EOS denial.
plain_english: J-1 visitors must apply to extend their stay with USCIS after sponsor approval; they can continue working while extension is pending; J-2 family can work only with permission and cannot support the J-1; if extension is denied, all must leave immediately; traveling while extension is pending does not cancel the application.
allowed: Continuation of employment/training for J-1 up to 240 days post admission expiration if EOS timely filed
J-1 program extension requests through RO and DOS
J-2 employment with USCIS authorization
Travel during pending EOS without abandonment
restricted_or_prohibited: J-2 employment to support J-1
J-2 EOS exceeding principal J-1 admission period
Employment after EOS denial
time_limits_or_durations: Up to 240 days employment authorization extension during pending EOS
EOS application must be filed within 30 days of DOS's reinstatement decision
EOS applications must be timely filed on or before expiration
evidence_quote: Like other nonimmigrants applying for EOS, they would need to file an EOS application on the form and in the manner designated by USCIS, with the required fee and in accordance with filing instructions, including any biometrics required by 8 CFR 103.16. [...] J–1 nonimmigrants seeking a program extension will continue to first request such an extension through the RO [...]. If such a program extension is recommended by the RO and approved by DOS, if necessary, the J–1 must apply for an EOS with USCIS to remain in the U.S. beyond the status expiration date on their I–94. [...] If an alien’s J–1 status has expired, but he or she timely filed an EOS application, DHS proposes to allow the alien to continue engaging in activities consistent with the terms and conditions of the alien’s program, including any employment authorization, beginning on the day after the admission period expires, for up to 240 days. [...] Unlike J–1 exchange visitors, J–2 spouses and eligible children may only engage in employment with authorization by USCIS. [...] DHS proposes to retain the current restriction on the J–2 dependent’s income described in 8 CFR 214.2(j)(1)(v)(A); the J–2 nonimmigrant’s income may be used to support the family’s customary recreational and cultural activities and related travel, among other things, but not to support the J–1. [...] A dependent J–2 spouse and children seeking to accompany the J–1 exchange visitor [...] would either need to be included on the primary applicant’s request for extension or file their own EOS applications [...]. If a J–1 exchange visitor is denied EOS, then the J–2 family members will also be denied EOS, and all will be required to leave the United States immediately. [...] DHS is using general terms [...] DHS proposes to allow J–1 nonimmigrants to continue employment or authorized training while an EOS application is pending with USCIS. Specifically, DHS proposes to allow J–1s who have properly filed an EOS on or before 6 months after the effective date of the final rule, to engage in the activities consistent with pursuing the terms and conditions of the exchange program objectives, including authorized training, while the EOS is pending, up to the DS–2019 end date filed with the EOS application. [...] DHS proposes not to consider travel during the time the EOS is pending to constitute abandonment of the EOS application.

policy_name: J-1 Reporting Requirements Update
affected_groups: J-1 exchange visitors and Responsible Officers (ROs)
current_policy: J-1 exchange visitors must report address changes within 10 calendar days; ROs update SEVIS within 21 days; term 'Service' used instead of USCIS.
proposed_change: Replace 'Service' with 'USCIS'; require J-1 exchange visitors to report changes of name and address within 10 calendar days; require ROs to update SEVIS within 10 business days; strike sentence referencing non-SEVIS programs.
plain_english: J-1 visitors must report address/name changes within 10 days; ROs must update SEVIS within 10 business days. Terminology updated to USCIS. Non-SEVIS program references removed.
time_limits_or_durations: 10 calendar days to report changes by J-1
10 business days for ROs to update SEVIS
evidence_quote: DHS proposes conforming amendments [...] replacing the term ‘Service’ with ‘USCIS’ and clarifying the number of days during which changes need to be reported by revising from 10 days to 10 ‘calendar’ days for exchange visitors to report changes in their names and addresses and from 21 days to 10 business days for the RO to update SEVIS, in order to conform with existing DOS regulations. [...] DHS proposes to strike the sentence which references non-SEVIS programs, as SEVIS enrollment is now a mandatory requirement.

policy_name: Definition and Eligibility Criteria for I Nonimmigrant Classification
affected_groups: I nonimmigrants (representatives of foreign information media)
current_policy: No codified regulatory definition requiring home office abroad for media organizations; long-standing practice distinguishes journalistic information from entertainment content.
proposed_change: Define foreign media organization as an entity engaged in regular gathering, production, or dissemination of journalistic information with a home office in a foreign country; codify that content must be primarily journalistic, not entertainment or promotional; require evidence (employment letter or attestation) verifying employment, work, remuneration, and foreign home office; clarify that content by bloggers must be on behalf of a qualifying foreign media organization to qualify as I nonimmigrant.
plain_english: To qualify for an I visa, you must work for a foreign media organization with a home office abroad and produce mainly news or educational content, not entertainment; you must provide proof of employment or freelance work meeting these criteria.
allowed: Representation of foreign media organizations with confirmed home office abroad
Content that is primarily journalistic, informational or educational
Freelance/self-employed with proper attestation
restricted_or_prohibited: Content primarily for entertainment (e.g., reality TV)
Personal blogs without representation by qualifying media organization
Promotional or marketing content
evidence_quote: DHS proposes to define a foreign media organization as ‘‘an organization engaged in the regular gathering, production or dissemination via print, radio, television, internet distribution, or other media, of journalistic information and has a home office in a foreign country.’’ [...] DHS is proposing to clarify and codify the DOS and USCIS long-standing practice interpreting ‘‘foreign information media’’ [...] as ‘‘journalistic information.’’ [...] In order to be granted I classification, an alien would need to meet his or her burden of proof [...] with a letter from the employing foreign media organization verifying the employment, the work to be performed, and the remuneration involved. [...] Where an alien is self-employed or freelancing, the alien must provide an attestation that verifies the employment, establishes that he or she is a representative of a qualifying foreign media organization that meets the foreign home office requirement, and describes the remuneration and work to be performed.

policy_name: Admission and Extension of Stay Periods for I Nonimmigrants with Special Conditions for PRC Passport Holders
affected_groups: I nonimmigrants, including those with passports from the People's Republic of China (PRC)
current_policy: No codified admission or extension period limits expressed as 240 or 90 days; employment authorized pending applications under specific conditions.
proposed_change: Set initial admission and EOS periods up to 240 days or until completion of assignment, whichever is shorter; for PRC passport holders (excluding Hong Kong and Macau SAR passports), admission and EOS periods limited to 90 days or assignment completion; allow continuation of activities consistent with I classification during timely EOS pending period up to 240/90 days; impose work cessation if EOS pending beyond authorized period unless approved; require timely filing of EOS applications to maintain status; deny extensions result in immediate departure without grace period and accrual of unlawful presence; dependents may be eligible for EOS under same conditions; multiple EOS applications allowed but work must cease pending approvals.
plain_english: I visa holders can stay up to 240 days (or 90 days for most PRC passport holders) per admission or extension; must file EOS timely to continue work; must stop work if extension not approved; failing to leave after denial starts unlawful stay. Dependents follow same rules.
allowed: Admission and extension up to 240 days or activity completion
Admission and extension up to 90 days for PRC passport holders (except HK/Macau)
Continue activities consistent with I classification during timely EOS pending periods
Multiple consecutive EOS applications if timely filed
restricted_or_prohibited: Work continuation beyond pending EOS period without prior approval
Extension periods exceeding set limits
Failure to leave immediately after EOS denial
exceptions: PRC passport holders (except HK/Macau SAR passports) limited to 90 days
time_limits_or_durations: Initial admission and EOS periods up to 240 days or activity completion
90 days admission/EOS for PRC passport holders except HK/Macau SAR
Timely filing required prior to expiration of current authorization
evidence_quote: DHS is proposing that aliens in I nonimmigrant classification have admission periods not to exceed 240 days or the period of time necessary to complete their activities, whichever is shorter [...]. However, I nonimmigrants presenting passports from the PRC (other than a Hong Kong SAR passport or Macau SAR passport) would be given admission and extension of stay periods of up to 90 days or until the activities or assignments consistent with the I classification are completed, whichever is shorter. [...] DHS proposes allowing an I nonimmigrant to continue activities consistent with the I classification while the timely application for EOS is pending, as provided for in 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(20), for a period not to exceed 240 days or the actual additional time requested on the EOS application, whichever is shorter (with the exception of an I nonimmigrant submitting a passport from the PRC [...], who can request extensions of up to 90 days). [...] If an EOS remains pending at the end of this period [...], DHS proposes the I nonimmigrant may remain so long as the EOS application is pending, and he or she has filed a subsequent EOS request [...] But DHS proposes that the alien cease working until his or her initial/preceding EOS application is approved. [...] The denial of an extension application requires the alien to cease work activities and depart the United States immediately. [...] Aliens applying for an EOS currently file a Form I–539 [...] DHS proposes that the dependents of an I nonimmigrant may be eligible for an EOS, under the same conditions and subject to the same restrictions as the principal I nonimmigrant.

policy_name: Fixed Period of Admission for F, J, and I Nonimmigrants
current_policy: F, J, and I nonimmigrants are admitted with duration of status (D/S) on Form I-94.
proposed_change: Replace D/S admission with a fixed period of admission tied to the program end date for F, J, and I nonimmigrants. The admission period will not exceed 4 years plus 30 days for departure or to seek lawful status. Unlawful presence will start accruing after the expiration of the fixed period of admission.
plain_english: Instead of staying in the U.S. for as long as their program lasts, certain visa holders will be allowed to stay only for a set time tied to their program end date plus a short grace period, with penalties for overstaying.
allowed: Entry up to the program end date plus 30 days grace period for F and J nonimmigrants who changed status before the final rule
Potential to request Extensions of Stay (EOS)
restricted_or_prohibited: Admission for indefinite duration (D/S) no longer allowed
Accrual of unlawful presence after fixed admission period expires
exceptions: Aliens granted change to F or J status before the final rule may be admitted per former practice up to the program end date plus 30 days
Underlying petitions with a pending change of status application may still be approved even if status change application is abandoned due to travel
time_limits_or_durations: Maximum 4 years admission plus 30 days grace period
Fixed periods replacing D/S admission
evidence_quote: DHS proposes to apply the same fixed period of admission applicable to aliens seeking to change from a different nonimmigrant status to, if eligible, I status. See proposed 8 CFR 214.2(i)(7)...aliens who were granted a change to F or J status before the effective date of the final rule, and are applying for admission as an F or J after the final rule’s effective date may be admitted up to the program end date as noted on the Form I–20 or DS–2019...not to exceed 4 years, plus a period of 30 days following their program end date...

policy_name: Abandonment of Change of Status Applications Upon Departure
affected_groups: Aliens applying for change of status
current_policy: Nonimmigrants can file applications to change status and may remain in the U.S. while application is pending. Departure during pendency may have unclear impact.
proposed_change: Codify longstanding policy that if an alien timely files a change of status application but departs the U.S. while the application is pending, USCIS will consider the application abandoned.
plain_english: If you apply to change your visa status but leave the U.S. before the decision is made, your application will be treated as if you gave up.
allowed: Underlying petitions filed along with the change of status may still be approved
Alien may obtain visa at U.S. Embassy/Consulate abroad to apply for admission in the new classification
restricted_or_prohibited: Change of status application considered abandoned if alien leaves U.S. while pending
exceptions: Approval of underlying petition notwithstanding abandonment of the change of status application
evidence_quote: DHS is proposing to codify the long-standing policy that, when an alien timely files an application to change to another nonimmigrant status, including F or J status, but departs the United States while the application is pending, USCIS will consider the application abandoned.

policy_name: Employment Authorization for I Nonimmigrants
current_policy: I nonimmigrants may be employed only for the sponsoring foreign news agency or bureau as stated in 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(10).
proposed_change: Cross-reference language in proposed 8 CFR 214.2(i) clarifying that I nonimmigrants may be employed in freelance or self-employment situations without a sponsoring news agency, provided they meet the requirements of working for a qualifying foreign media organization.
plain_english: Foreign media visa holders can work freelance or for themselves if they prove they work for a qualifying foreign media organization, even if they don't have a formal sponsor.
allowed: Employment for sponsoring foreign news agency or bureau
Freelance and self-employment for qualifying foreign media organizations
evidence_quote: DHS proposes to cross-reference language in proposed 8 CFR 214.2(i) for I nonimmigrants, which clarifies that limitations currently in the provision... allow for freelance and self-employment situations where the I nonimmigrant may not have a 'sponsoring' foreign news agency or bureau...

policy_name: Biometrics Requirement for Extensions of Stay
current_policy: Applicants filing Form I-539 may be required to submit biometrics, but details vary among classifications.
proposed_change: Applicants filing for an extension of stay (EOS), including for the I nonimmigrant status, might be required to submit biometrics under proposed 8 CFR 214.2(i)(5).
plain_english: People applying to extend their stay might need to provide fingerprints or other biometric data.
allowed: Filing of Form I-539 with biometrics as required
evidence_quote: And, as with other applicants who file a Form I–539, under the proposed rule applicants might be required to submit biometrics. See proposed 8 CFR 214.2(i)(5).

policy_name: Elimination of Duration of Status Admission for F, J, and I Nonimmigrants
affected_groups: I nonimmigrant representatives of foreign information media
current_policy: F-1, J-1, and I nonimmigrants are admitted for Duration of Status (D/S), allowing them to remain in the U.S. for the duration of their program without a fixed end date.
proposed_change: DHS proposes to eliminate the practice of admitting F-1, J-1, and I nonimmigrant classifications for Duration of Status (D/S). Instead, these nonimmigrants will be admitted for a fixed period required to complete their academic program, foreign information media employment, or exchange program, not exceeding the periods defined in the new rule. Extensions of stay beyond the admission period granted at entry will require filing for extension with USCIS.
plain_english: Students and exchange visitors will no longer be allowed to stay in the U.S. indefinitely while their program is ongoing. They will be given a fixed period of time based on their program length and will need to apply to extend their stay if needed.
allowed: Admission for period necessary to complete program, up to fixed maximums
Extension of stay by application to USCIS
restricted_or_prohibited: Admission for Duration of Status (D/S) no longer allowed for F, J, and I nonimmigrants
exceptions: Transition provisions allow aliens maintaining status before effective date to remain until the later of EAD expiration or program end date, up to 4 years; extensions permitted via application
time_limits_or_durations: F nonimmigrants can be admitted up to 4 years or the length of the program as specified on Form I-20, whichever is shorter
30 days before program start and 30 days after program end (not counted toward max stay)
F-1 students in English language training limited to 24 months plus 30-day departure period
Public high school F-1 students limited to 12 months total

policy_name: F-1 Student 30-day Grace Period and Departure Rules

The 30-day period is reflected on Form I-94. Withdrawn students have 15 days to depart. Failure to maintain full course work means no additional departure time.
